comments.text: Greetings from Reno! My mother became hypochondriac due to her search for what was really wrong with her. Her tenacity and the fact that she was going to university in  Baltimore in the 1950's saved her. She fell into a coma on campus her sophomore year, and was taken to John Hopkins, where she was diagnosed with three conditions, two of which were new to medical the scene: clinical hypoglycemia, hypothyroidism, and injury caused epilepsy. She had been told since she was fifteen that her frequent fainting and seizures were attention seeking devises. I credit her with teaching me how to aggressively advocate for myself and others, even though she never was able to stop the search herself, unfortunately, which ended up causing her quite a bit of harm.

comments.text: Here's my story of how I ended up in a coma and ultimatly, a wheelchair, all because of criminal negligence of nurses and doctors. I've had seizures and movement disorders all troughout my childhood. They were horrible, and I was in hospital more often than any child should. The doctors did all the usual tests. EEG, MRI. Nothing. So they sent me to a psychiatrist. Who sent me back to the hospital. Who sent me back to the psychiatrist. And so I went back and forth. Until the hospital staff was really annoyed every time I arrived in the ER. They didn't even give me medicine anymore. One time, I was in a seizure for ONE HOUR. My mom called for the nurses for like a hundred times. They had put my heartrate monitor on quiet and removed the call button from our room. Then I must have seized so badly, that I fell out of the bed. OVER the side guards they pulled up. I landed badly on my hip, and vomited. I aspirated some of the vomit. When I turned blue, my mom ran out and was intent on pulling a nurse inside my room by her hair if necessary, but they did actually finally respond to my low oxygen rating, which was 40% at the lowest point (my mom told me, she said she was so afraid I'd have brain damage, I was incedibly lucky) and then all hell broke loose. They intubated me and I was in a coma for a week. (I had aspiration induced pneumonia) When I woke up, I found that I couldn't walk anymore. I still can't. After all this was over, I was sent to a clinic specifically for epilepsy. There, I was diagnosed with Frontal Lobe Epilepsy. The doctor there told me, that form of epilepsy is very hard to diagnose and hard to spot in EEGs, sometimes it doesn't show typcal changes unless the patient has a seizure AT THAT MOMENT. Still, the way I was treated, ignored, like I was just throwing a tantrum... only because they couldn't find the answer in an EEG... Has destroyed my life.

comments.text: I was born with no thyroid and have been on replacement hormones my entire life. I immediately noticed the symptoms of hypothyroidism and tried to communicate them but my doctor would not listen to me. I was underdosed ages 12-17 until my physical and mental health got so bad I was hospitalized for 2 weeks. The first change they made was to give me double the levothyroxin. My mental health was already so much better after just a week. After my hospitalization, I was able to get a new endocrinologist and my dose ended up being triple the amount I was originally on. Being denied these incredibly important growth hormones during my adolescence caused me to mature much slower than my peers. i even lost my period. I am in my 20s now have the right medication! Life is 100% better.

My doctors have gaslit me more times than I can count.

One doctor refused to give me a hysterectomy because he felt I was "too young." Never mind that I am almost 39, went through puberty at 8 years old, and I'd had 10 pregnancies, 6 births, with 5 living children. I was dealing with extremely long, painful periods, and he decided the solution was an IUD.

I eventually saw another OB-GYN and asked her about a hysterectomy. She agreed I was a good candidate because I was experiencing something called adenomyosis (thickening of the uterine lining, which causes the tissue to grow into my uterine walls, causing severe pain and bleeding), and put me on the surgery schedule.

Then the first doctor found out and called me and said, "I thought we agreed on the IUD? And you agreed you weren't a good candidate for a hysterectomy."

I told him, "No, you agreed and decided those things for me."

I did end up getting the hysterectomy (by the first doctor), but he refused to remove my ovaries, even though they were causing me pain and still do. Then he had the nerve to tell me that ovaries don't cause pain. 😑
